Money and Credit

Money is fascinating and full of curiosities — from grains and cattle to coins, currency, cheques and UPI. This chapter explains modern money and the banking system, then turns to credit: its terms, its two faces, formal and informal lenders, and self-help groups.

Chapter Overview

What this chapter is about, at a glance

The use of money spans a very large part of our everyday life. In many transactions goods are bought and sold with money, in some services are exchanged for money, and in some there is no actual transfer now but a promise to pay later.

Money is accepted because a person holding money can easily exchange it for any commodity or service. In a barter system goods are exchanged directly, and this requires a double coincidence of wants — what one person wishes to sell must be exactly what the other wishes to buy. Money, by providing a crucial intermediate step, eliminates the need for a double coincidence of wants and acts as a medium of exchange.

The chapter then explains modern forms of money — currency, which is authorised by the government and issued by the Reserve Bank of India, and demand deposits with banks, which can be withdrawn on demand and used for payments by cheque. Banks keep only a small proportion of deposits as cash and use the rest to lend; the difference between the interest charged on loans and paid on deposits is their main source of income.

The second half is about credit: two contrasting stories — Salim the shoe manufacturer, for whom credit works, and Swapna the farmer, who falls into a debt trap. It explains the terms of credit, the variety of credit arrangements in a village called Sonpur, the difference between formal and informal sources, and how self-help groups help the poor borrow without collateral.

Double coincidence of wants

The situation in barter where what one person wishes to sell is exactly what the other wishes to buy.

Currency

Paper notes and coins. Modern currency has no use of its own; it is accepted because it is authorised by the government.

Who issues currency

The Reserve Bank of India issues currency notes on behalf of the central government; no other individual or organisation may do so.

Demand deposits

Deposits in bank accounts that can be withdrawn on demand; with cheques they share the essential features of money.

Bank cash

Banks in India hold about 5 per cent of their deposits as cash to meet withdrawals.

Credit

An agreement in which the lender supplies the borrower with money, goods or services in return for a promise of future payment.

Terms of credit

Interest rate, collateral and documentation requirement, and the mode of repayment.

Formal vs informal

Formal: banks and cooperatives, supervised by the RBI. Informal: moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives and friends — no supervisor.

Self-help groups

15–20 members, usually women of one neighbourhood, who save regularly, lend to each other, and later get bank loans without collateral.

Money as a Medium of Exchange

The use of money spans a very large part of our everyday life. In many transactions goods are bought and sold with the use of money; in some, services are exchanged with money; and for some there might not be any actual transfer of money now but a promise to pay money later.

Why are transactions made in money? A person holding money can easily exchange it for any commodity or service that he or she might want. Take a shoe manufacturer who wants to sell shoes and buy wheat. He first exchanges shoes for money, then exchanges the money for wheat. Imagine how much more difficult it would be if he had to directly exchange shoes for wheat: he would have to look for a wheat-growing farmer who not only wants to sell wheat but also wants to buy shoes in exchange — both parties would have to agree to sell and buy each other’s commodities.

Definition

Double coincidence of wants: what a person desires to sell is exactly what the other wishes to buy. In a barter system, where goods are directly exchanged without the use of money, double coincidence of wants is an essential feature.

In an economy where money is in use, money — by providing the crucial intermediate step — eliminates the need for double coincidence of wants. It is no longer necessary for the shoe manufacturer to look for a farmer who will buy his shoes and at the same time sell him wheat; all he has to do is find a buyer for his shoes, and then he can purchase wheat or anything else. Since money acts as an intermediate in the exchange process, it is called a medium of exchange.

Let’s work these out

How does the use of money make it easier to exchange things? Can you think of examples of goods or services being exchanged, or wages paid, through barter?

Modern Forms of Money

Before the introduction of coins, a variety of objects was used as money. Since the very early ages, Indians used grains and cattle as money. Thereafter came the use of metallic coins — gold, silver and copper — a phase which continued well into the last century. The chapter shows early punch-marked coins (perhaps 2,500 years old), Gupta coins, a Tughlaq coin, a gold mohar from Akbar’s reign and a modern coin.

Currency

Modern forms of money include currency — paper notes and coins. Unlike the things used as money earlier, modern currency is not made of precious metal such as gold, silver and copper, and unlike grain and cattle it is of no everyday use. The modern currency is without any use of its own.

Then why is it accepted as a medium of exchange? Because the currency is authorised by the government of the country. In India, the Reserve Bank of India issues currency notes on behalf of the central government. As per Indian law, no other individual or organisation is allowed to issue currency. Moreover, the law legalises the use of the rupee as a medium of payment that cannot be refused in settling transactions in India — no individual in India can legally refuse a payment made in rupees. Hence the rupee is widely accepted.

Deposits with banks

The other form in which people hold money is as deposits with banks. At any point of time people need only some currency for their day-to-day needs — workers who receive salaries at the end of each month have extra cash at the beginning of the month. They deposit it with banks by opening an account; banks accept the deposits and pay an amount as interest, so the money is safe and earns interest, and people can withdraw it as and when required. Since the deposits in bank accounts can be withdrawn on demand, these deposits are called demand deposits.

Teacher explanation

Why are demand deposits considered money? Because they can be withdrawn on demand and — through cheques — used to settle payments directly, without cash. Along with currency, demand deposits constitute money in the modern economy.

Cheque Payments and the Loan Activities of Banks

A shoe manufacturer, M. Salim, has to make a payment to the leather supplier and writes a cheque for a specific amount. This means he instructs his bank to pay this amount to the leather supplier. The supplier takes the cheque and deposits it in his own account; the money is transferred from one bank account to another in a couple of days, and the transaction is complete without any payment of cash.

Definition

Cheque: a paper instructing the bank to pay a specific amount from the person’s account to the person in whose name the cheque has been issued. The facility of cheques against demand deposits makes it possible to directly settle payments without the use of cash.

Demand deposits share the essential features of money, and since they are accepted widely as a means of payment, along with currency they constitute money in the modern economy. But for the banks there would be no demand deposits and no payments by cheques — the modern forms of money, currency and deposits, are closely linked to the working of the modern banking system.

What do banks do with the deposits?

Banks keep only a small proportion of their deposits as cash with themselves — banks in India these days hold about 5 per cent of their deposits as cash — as a provision to pay depositors who might come to withdraw money on any given day. Since only some of the many depositors come to withdraw cash on any particular day, the bank is able to manage with this cash.

Banks use the major portion of the deposits to extend loans, because there is a huge demand for loans for various economic activities. In this way banks mediate between those who have surplus funds (the depositors) and those who are in need of these funds (the borrowers). Banks charge a higher interest rate on loans than what they offer on deposits; the difference between what is charged from borrowers and what is paid to depositors is their main source of income.

Think about it

What do you think would happen if all the depositors went to ask for their money at the same time? — The bank would be unable to pay, because it holds only about 5 per cent as cash and has lent the rest. This is why banks must be regulated and supervised — the role played by the Reserve Bank of India.

Let’s work these out

M. Salim wants to withdraw Rs 20,000 in cash. How would he write a cheque to withdraw money? After the transaction between Salim and Prem, whose balance increases and whose decreases? Why are demand deposits considered money?

Credit — Two Different Situations
Definition

Credit (loan): an agreement in which the lender supplies the borrower with money, goods or services in return for the promise of future payment.

(1) Festival season — Salim’s case

It is festival season two months from now and the shoe manufacturer, Salim, has received an order from a large trader for 3,000 pairs of shoes to be delivered in a month. To complete production on time he has to hire a few more workers for stitching and pasting and purchase raw materials. To meet these expenses Salim obtains loans from two sources: he asks the leather supplier to supply leather now and promises to pay later; and he obtains a loan in cash from the large trader as advance payment for 1,000 pairs of shoes, promising to deliver the whole order by the end of the month. At the end of the month Salim delivers the order, makes a good profit and repays the money he had borrowed.

In this case credit plays a vital and positive role: Salim obtains credit to meet the working capital needs of production; it helps him meet ongoing expenses, complete production on time and thereby increase his earnings.

(2) Swapna’s problem

Swapna, a small farmer, grows groundnut on her three acres. She takes a loan from the moneylender to meet the expenses of cultivation, hoping her harvest will repay the loan. Midway through the season the crop is hit by pests and fails; though she sprays expensive pesticides it makes little difference. She is unable to repay the moneylender and the debt grows over the year into a large amount. Next year she takes a fresh loan for cultivation; it is a normal crop this year, but the earnings are not enough to cover the old loan. She is caught in debt and has to sell a part of the land to pay off the debt.

In Swapna’s case, the failure of the crop made loan repayment impossible. Credit, instead of helping her improve her earnings, left her worse off. This is an example of what is commonly called a debt trap — credit pushes the borrower into a situation from which recovery is very painful.

Key conclusion

Whether credit would be useful or not depends on the risks in the situation and whether there is some support in case of loss. In one situation credit increases earnings and the person is better off; in another, because of crop failure, credit pushes the person into a debt trap.

In rural areas the main demand for credit is for crop production, which involves considerable costs on seeds, fertilisers, pesticides, water, electricity and repair of equipment. There is a minimum stretch of three to four months between buying these inputs and selling the crop. Farmers usually take crop loans at the beginning of the season and repay after harvest — so repayment is crucially dependent on the income from farming.

Comparing the two credit situations
SalimSwapna
Why did they need credit?To meet working capital needs — hire workers, buy raw material, complete an order on timeTo meet the expenses of cultivation — seeds, fertiliser, pesticides
What was the risk?Not completing the order on time; but the order was from a large trader with an advanceCrop failure due to pests; earnings then insufficient to repay
What was the outcome?Delivered the order, made a good profit and repaid the loan — better offDebt grew, had to sell part of the land — caught in a debt trap
Terms of Credit

Every loan agreement specifies an interest rate which the borrower must pay to the lender along with the repayment of the principal. In addition, lenders may demand collateral (security) against loans.

Definition

Collateral: an asset that the borrower owns (such as land, building, vehicle, livestock, deposits with banks) and uses as a guarantee to a lender until the loan is repaid. If the borrower fails to repay, the lender has the right to sell the asset or collateral to obtain payment.

Interest rate, collateral and documentation requirement, and the mode of repayment together comprise what is called the terms of credit. The terms of credit vary substantially from one credit arrangement to another, depending on the nature of the lender and the borrower.

A house loan

Megha’s house loan: Megha has taken a loan of Rs 5 lakh from the bank to purchase a house. The annual interest rate is 12 per cent and the loan is to be repaid in 10 years in monthly instalments. Megha had to submit documents showing her employment records and salary before the bank agreed to the loan. The bank retained as collateral the papers of the new house, which will be returned only when she repays the entire loan with interest.

Megha’s housing loan — fill-in details

Fill in the blanks

While taking a loan, borrowers look for easy terms of credit — low interest rate, easy conditions for repayment, less collateral and documentation requirements.

Variety of Credit Arrangements — the Village of Sonpur

Rohit and Ranjan wanted to know the credit arrangements in their area: who provided credit, who borrowed, and on what terms. On 15 November 2019 they visited the fields of Sonpur, a small irrigated village planted with potato crops.

Three borrowers in Sonpur and their terms of credit
BorrowerSource and termsPurpose
Shyamal — small farmer, 1.5 acresEarlier the village moneylender at 5% per month (60% a year); for the last few years an agricultural trader at 3% per month, who also makes him promise to sell the crop to himCultivation — inputs supplied on credit at the start of the season
Arun — medium farmer, 7 acresOne of the few in Sonpur to get a bank loan: 8.5% per annum, repayable anytime in the next three years; can later borrow again against a cold storage receiptCultivation; store the rest of the potatoes and sell later
Rama — agricultural labourer, landlessDepends on her employer, a medium landowner, at 5% per month, repaying by working for him; often takes a fresh loan before the old one is repaid; owes Rs 5,000Daily expenses in months without work, sudden illness, family functions

Besides the interest charge, the trader also makes farmers promise to sell the crop to him, which ensures prompt repayment; and since crop prices are low after harvest, the trader profits by buying low and selling later when the price has risen. Arun, with a bank loan at 8.5 per cent and the option of a cold storage receipt loan, can wait for a better price. Rama, with no collateral and no alternative, depends entirely on her employer: the only source of credit for landless people in Sonpur is the landowner-employers.

Loans from Cooperatives

Besides banks, the other major source of cheap credit in rural areas is cooperative societies. Members of a cooperative pool their resources for cooperation in certain areas. There are several types of cooperatives — farmers’ cooperatives, weavers’ cooperatives, industrial workers’ cooperatives.

Krishak Cooperative functions in a village not very far from Sonpur. It has 2,300 farmers as members. It accepts deposits from its members; with these deposits as collateral the cooperative has obtained a large loan from the bank, and these funds are used to provide loans to members. Once these loans are repaid, another round of lending can take place. Krishak Cooperative provides loans for the purchase of agricultural implements, for cultivation and agricultural trade, fishery loans, loans for construction of houses and for a variety of other expenses.

Let’s work these out

List the various sources of credit in Sonpur. Compare the terms of credit for the small farmer, the medium farmer and the landless agricultural worker. Why will Arun have a higher income from cultivation than Shyamal? Can everyone in Sonpur get credit at a cheap rate?

Teacher explanation

Answer: the sources in Sonpur are the moneylender, the agricultural trader, the bank, the employer-landowner and the cooperative. Shyamal pays 3% a month (36% a year) and must sell to the trader; Arun pays 8.5% a year and can wait for a good price; Rama pays 5% a month and repays with labour, often borrowing again before repaying. Arun earns more because cheap credit and storage let him avoid distress sales. No — only those with collateral and documents, like Arun, get cheap credit.

Formal Sector Credit in India

Loans can be grouped as formal sector loans and informal sector loans. Among the former are loans from banks and cooperatives; the informal lenders include moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives and friends.

Graph 1 — Sources of credit in rural India, 2019
SourceShare
Commercial banks51%
Moneylenders23%
Cooperative banks and societies10%
Relatives and friends7%
Other formal agencies5%
Other informal agencies3%
Landlords1%

More credit comes from the formal sector than from the informal — but the informal sector still supplies a large part. The Reserve Bank of India supervises the functioning of formal sources of loans: banks maintain a minimum cash balance out of the deposits they receive, and the RBI monitors that they actually do so. Similarly, the RBI sees that banks give loans not just to profit-making businesses and traders but also to small cultivators, small-scale industries and small borrowers, and periodically banks must submit information to the RBI on how much they are lending, to whom and at what interest rate.

By contrast, there is no organisation which supervises the credit activities of lenders in the informal sector. They can lend at whatever interest rate they choose; there is no one to stop them from using unfair means to get their money back. Compared with formal lenders, most informal lenders charge a much higher interest, so the cost of borrowing is much higher.

Higher cost of borrowing means a larger part of the earnings of borrowers is used to repay the loan, so they have less income left for themselves (as with Shyamal). In certain cases the high interest rate can mean that the amount to be repaid is greater than the income of the borrower — leading to increasing debt (as with Rama) and a debt trap. Also, people who might wish to start an enterprise by borrowing may not do so because of the high cost of borrowing.

For these reasons, banks and cooperative societies need to lend more. This would lead to higher incomes and many people could then borrow cheaply for a variety of needs — grow crops, do business, set up small-scale industries. Cheap and affordable credit is crucial for the country’s development.

Formal and Informal Credit — Who Gets What?

Graph 2 shows the importance of formal and informal sources of credit for people in urban areas, dividing people into four groups from poor to rich.

Graph 2 — Of all loans taken by urban households, what percentage was formal and what informal?
GroupFrom informal sourcesFrom formal sources
Poor households54%46%
Households with a few assetsLower than the poorHigher than the poor
Well-off householdsLower stillHigher still
Rich households17%83%

A similar pattern is found in rural areas. The rich households are availing cheap credit from formal lenders whereas the poor households have to pay a large amount for borrowing.

What does this suggest? First, the formal sector still meets only about half of the total credit needs of the rural people; the remaining credit needs are met from informal sources. Second, while formal sector loans need to expand, it is also necessary that everyone receives these loans — at present it is the richer households who receive formal credit, whereas the poor depend on informal sources. It is important that formal credit is distributed more equally so that the poor can benefit from cheaper loans.

Self-Help Groups for the Poor

Why are poor households still dependent on informal sources? Banks are not present everywhere in rural India, and even when they are, getting a loan from a bank is much more difficult than from informal sources: as with Megha, bank loans require proper documents and collateral. Absence of collateral is one of the major reasons which prevents the poor from getting bank loans. Informal lenders such as moneylenders know the borrowers personally and are often willing to give a loan without collateral; borrowers can, if necessary, approach them even without repaying earlier loans. But moneylenders charge very high rates of interest, keep no records of transactions and harass the poor borrowers.

In recent years people have tried newer ways of providing loans to the poor. The idea is to organise the rural poor, in particular women, into small Self Help Groups (SHGs) and pool their savings.

  • A typical SHG has 15–20 members, usually belonging to one neighbourhood, who meet and save regularly.
  • Saving per member varies from Rs 25 to Rs 100 or more, depending on the ability of the people to save.
  • Members can take small loans from the group itself; the group charges interest, but less than what a moneylender charges.
  • After a year or two, if the group is regular in savings, it becomes eligible for a loan from the bank.
  • The loan is sanctioned in the name of the group and is meant to create self-employment opportunities for members — releasing mortgaged land, meeting working capital needs (seeds, fertilisers, bamboo, cloth), housing materials, or acquiring assets such as a sewing machine, handloom or cattle.
  • Most important decisions about savings and loan activities are taken by the group members: the purpose, amount, interest and repayment schedule. The group is responsible for repayment, and any non-repayment by a member is followed up seriously by the others.

Because of this feature, banks are willing to lend to poor women organised in SHGs even though they have no collateral. Thus SHGs help borrowers overcome the problem of lack of collateral: they can get timely loans for a variety of purposes at a reasonable interest rate. Moreover, SHGs are the building blocks of organisation of the rural poor — not only do they help women become financially self-reliant, the regular meetings provide a platform to discuss and act on social issues such as health, nutrition and domestic violence.

Grameen Bank

Grameen Bank of Bangladesh: “If credit can be made available to the poor people on terms and conditions that are appropriate and reasonable, these millions of small people with their millions of small pursuits can add up to create the biggest development wonder.” — Professor Muhammad Yunus, founder of Grameen Bank and recipient of the 2006 Nobel Prize for Peace. Started in the 1970s as a small project, Grameen Bank in 2018 had over 9 million members in about 81,600 villages across Bangladesh. Almost all the borrowers are women from the poorest sections, and they have proved that poor women are reliable borrowers who can start and run small income-generating activities.

Summing Up

We have looked at the modern forms of money and how they are linked with the banking system. On one side are the depositors who keep their money in banks, and on the other side the borrowers who take loans. Economic activities require loans or credit. Credit can have a positive impact, or in certain situations make the borrower worse off.

Credit is available from a variety of sources — formal and informal — and terms of credit vary substantially between them. At present it is the richer households who receive credit from formal sources whereas the poor depend on informal sources. It is essential that total formal sector credit increases so that dependence on the more expensive informal credit becomes less, and that the poor get a much greater share of formal loans from banks and cooperative societies. Both these steps are important for development.

Flashcards

All key terms

Key terms and definitions
TermSimple explanation
Barter systemDirect exchange of goods without the use of money; it requires a double coincidence of wants.
Double coincidence of wantsA situation where what a person wishes to sell is exactly what the other wishes to buy.
Medium of exchangeMoney’s role as the intermediate step in exchange, which removes the need for a double coincidence of wants.
CurrencyPaper notes and coins; modern currency has no use of its own and is accepted because the government authorises it.
Reserve Bank of IndiaThe body that issues currency notes on behalf of the central government and supervises the functioning of formal sources of loans.
Demand depositsDeposits in bank accounts that can be withdrawn on demand; with cheques they are used as money.
ChequeA paper instructing the bank to pay a specific amount from a person’s account to the person named on it.
Credit (loan)An agreement in which the lender supplies the borrower with money, goods or services in return for a promise of future payment.
PrincipalThe amount borrowed, which must be repaid along with interest.
Interest rateThe charge the borrower pays to the lender, expressed as a percentage, along with repayment of the principal.
CollateralAn asset the borrower owns and offers as a guarantee until the loan is repaid; if repayment fails, the lender may sell it.
Terms of creditInterest rate, collateral and documentation requirement, and mode of repayment, taken together.
Debt trapA situation in which credit pushes the borrower into debt from which recovery is very painful, often forcing the sale of assets such as land.
Formal sector creditLoans from banks and cooperative societies, supervised by the RBI.
Informal sector creditLoans from moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives and friends; unsupervised, usually at much higher interest.
Cooperative societyAn association whose members pool resources; it accepts deposits, borrows from banks using them as collateral, and lends to members.
Self Help Group (SHG)A group of 15–20 people, usually women of one neighbourhood, who save regularly, lend small amounts to each other and later obtain bank loans without collateral.
Grameen BankA Bangladesh bank founded by Muhammad Yunus that lends to the poor, mainly women; it had over 9 million members in about 81,600 villages in 2018.
Working capitalMoney needed for the ongoing expenses of production — raw material, wages — which is what Salim’s credit financed.

NCERT In-text Questions and Answers

The questions printed inside the chapter

These are the “Can you…” and activity questions that appear inside the chapter text. Model answers are based on the chapter itself.

1.

How does the use of money make it easier to exchange things?

Model answer

Money acts as an intermediate in exchange: a seller need only find someone with money, not someone who has exactly what he wants to buy. This removes the double coincidence of wants. The shoe manufacturer sells shoes for money and then buys wheat with it, without having to find a farmer who wants shoes.

2.

Can you think of some examples of goods or services being exchanged, or wages being paid, through barter?

Model answer

In villages, labour is sometimes paid in grain; a carpenter may be paid with a share of the harvest; neighbours exchange farm labour during sowing and harvesting; a barber may be paid in grain each season. (Student answers will vary.)

3.

M. Salim wants to withdraw Rs 20,000 in cash. How would he write a cheque to withdraw money?

Model answer

He would fill in the date, write his own name as the payee (“self”), write “Rupees Twenty Thousand only” and the figure Rs 20,000, sign the cheque, and present it at the bank counter — the bank then pays him the cash from his account.

4.

After the transaction between Salim and Prem, (i) Salim’s balance increases and Prem’s increases (ii) Salim’s balance decreases and Prem’s increases (iii) Salim’s balance increases and Prem’s decreases.

Model answer

(ii) Salim’s balance decreases and Prem’s increases. The money is transferred from Salim’s account to Prem’s.

5.

Why are demand deposits considered as money?

Model answer

Because they can be withdrawn on demand and can be used to settle payments directly through cheques, without cash. They are widely accepted as a means of payment, so along with currency they constitute money in the modern economy.

6.

Fill the table for Salim and Swapna: why did they need credit, what was the risk, what was the outcome?

Model answer

Salim: needed credit to hire workers and buy raw material to complete a large order; the risk was failing to deliver on time; the outcome was a good profit and repayment. Swapna: needed credit for cultivation expenses; the risk was crop failure from pests; the outcome was mounting debt, sale of part of her land, and a debt trap.

7.

Supposing Salim continues to get orders from traders, what would be his position after 6 years?

Model answer

He would be able to expand production, employ more workers, buy better equipment and build a reputation for timely delivery. His earnings and creditworthiness would rise, and he might need less borrowing per order because his own working capital would grow.

8.

What are the reasons that make Swapna’s situation so risky? Discuss factors — pesticides; role of moneylenders; climate.

Model answer

Pesticides: they are expensive and may not work, so costs rise without saving the crop. Moneylenders: interest is very high, there is no flexibility when a crop fails, and no insurance — the debt simply grows. Climate: rain-fed groundnut depends on rainfall, so one bad season destroys repayment capacity. Together they mean the risk of failure falls entirely on the borrower.

9.

Why do lenders ask for collateral while lending?

Model answer

As security: if the borrower fails to repay, the lender can sell the asset to recover the money. It reduces the lender’s risk, which is why banks insist on it — and why the poor, who own little, find bank loans hard to get.

10.

Given that a large number of people in our country are poor, does it in any way affect their capacity to borrow?

Model answer

Yes. Because they own little collateral and often lack proper documents, banks are unwilling to lend to them, so they must borrow from informal lenders at very high interest — which further reduces their income and can push them into a debt trap.

11.

Fill in the blanks choosing the correct option: While taking a loan, borrowers look for easy terms of credit. This means ___ (low/high) interest rate, ___ (easy/tough) conditions for repayment, ___ (less/more) collateral and documentation requirements.

Model answer

Low interest rate, easy conditions for repayment, less collateral and documentation.

12.

List the various sources of credit in Sonpur. Underline the various uses of credit in Sonpur. Compare the terms of credit for the small farmer, the medium farmer and the landless agricultural worker.

Model answer

Sources: the village moneylender, the agricultural trader, the bank, the landowner-employer and (nearby) the Krishak Cooperative. Uses: cultivation inputs, storage and marketing, daily household expenses in months without work, illness and family functions. Terms: Shyamal (small farmer) pays 3% a month and must sell to the trader; Arun (medium farmer) pays 8.5% a year with documents and can store his crop; Rama (landless) pays 5% a month, repays with labour and has no alternative.

13.

Why will Arun have a higher income from cultivation compared to Shyamal?

Model answer

Because Arun gets cheap bank credit at 8.5 per cent a year and can store potatoes in a cold storage and borrow against the receipt, so he is not forced to sell immediately at low post-harvest prices. Shyamal pays 3 per cent a month and must sell his crop to the trader who lent to him, losing the benefit of higher later prices.

14.

Can everyone in Sonpur get credit at a cheap rate? Who are the people who can?

Model answer

No. Only those with collateral, documents and some land — like Arun — get cheap bank credit. Small farmers get trader credit at high interest with a condition to sell to the lender, and landless workers depend on employers at 5 per cent a month.

15.

Tick the correct answer. (i) Over the years, Rama’s debt: will rise / will remain constant / will decline. (ii) Arun is one of the few people in Sonpur to take a bank loan because: other people prefer to borrow from moneylenders / banks demand collateral which everyone cannot provide / the interest rate on bank loans is the same as that charged by traders.

Model answer

(i) Will rise — she takes a fresh loan before repaying the old one. (ii) Banks demand collateral which everyone cannot provide.

16.

Talk to some people to find out the credit arrangements that exist in your area. Note the differences in the terms of credit across people.

Model answer

Ask each person: who lent the money, how much, at what interest, for how long, what was pledged, and what happens if repayment fails. You will usually find that those with property and salary papers borrow from banks at 8–12 per cent a year, while those without borrow from moneylenders or traders at 3–10 per cent a month. (Student activity.)

17.

What are the differences between formal and informal sources of credit?

Model answer

Formal sources are banks and cooperatives, supervised by the RBI, charging lower interest and requiring collateral and documents; informal sources are moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives and friends, unsupervised, charging much higher interest and often lending without collateral but sometimes using unfair means to recover.

18.

Why should credit at reasonable rates be available for all?

Model answer

Because credit is needed for cultivation, business and emergencies, and cheap credit raises incomes while expensive credit reduces them and can cause a debt trap. It is also a matter of equity: the poor currently pay the most for credit, which keeps them poor. Cheap and affordable credit is crucial for the country’s development.

19.

Should there be a supervisor, such as the RBI, that looks into the loan activities of informal lenders? Why would its task be quite difficult?

Model answer

In principle yes — supervision would protect borrowers from very high interest and unfair recovery. But it is very difficult in practice: informal lenders are numerous, small and unregistered; they operate in villages and neighbourhoods without records; loans are often oral and in cash; and borrowers may not complain because they need the lender again.

20.

Why do you think that the share of formal sector credit is higher for the richer households compared to the poorer households?

Model answer

Because formal lenders require collateral and documentation, which only those with assets and regular incomes can provide; the rich also borrow larger amounts, which banks find worth the paperwork. The poor, without collateral, are left to informal lenders who know them personally.

08

NCERT Exercise Questions and Answers

End-of-chapter exercises, projects and activities

NCERT Exercises

Reproduced from the exercise section of the chapter, with model answers. Word limits are the ones the textbook sets.

1.
NCERT exercise3 marks

In situations with high risks, credit might create further problems for the borrower. Explain.

Model answer

In high-risk situations — like Swapna’s rain-fed groundnut crop hit by pests — the borrower may be unable to repay, and the interest keeps accumulating. The debt then grows beyond the borrower’s income, forcing the sale of assets such as land. Credit that was meant to raise earnings ends by making the borrower worse off: this is a debt trap. The risk is greatest when there is no insurance or support in case of loss and when the lender charges very high interest.

2.
NCERT exercise3 marks

How does money solve the problem of double coincidence of wants? Explain with an example of your own.

Model answer

Money provides an intermediate step, so a seller needs only a buyer with money, not a buyer who has exactly the goods the seller wants. Example: a carpenter who wants rice sells his table for money to anyone who wants a table, and then uses the money to buy rice from any shop. Without money he would have to find a rice farmer who wanted a table.

3.
NCERT exercise3 marks

How do banks mediate between those who have surplus money and those who need money?

Model answer

Banks accept deposits from those with surplus money and pay them interest; they keep about 5 per cent as cash for withdrawals and lend the rest to borrowers, charging a higher interest. The difference between the two rates is their main source of income. In this way they channel savings into loans for cultivation, business and industry.

4.
NCERT exercise2 marks

Look at a 10 rupee note. What is written on top? Can you explain this statement?

Model answer

It says “Reserve Bank of India” — and the note is issued by the RBI on behalf of the central government. This is why it is accepted: Indian law authorises the RBI alone to issue currency, and legalises the rupee as a medium of payment that cannot be refused in settling transactions in India. The promise is printed on behalf of the Governor.

5.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Why do we need to expand formal sources of credit in India?

Model answer

Because informal lenders charge much higher interest, keep no records and can use unfair means to recover; high-cost borrowing reduces borrowers’ incomes, can cause a debt trap and discourages enterprise. Formal credit is cheaper and supervised by the RBI, yet it meets only about half of rural credit needs and goes mainly to richer households. Expanding formal credit — and distributing it more equally — would raise incomes and support development.

6.
NCERT exercise5 marks

What is the basic idea behind the SHGs for the poor? Explain in your own words.

Model answer

That the poor can borrow cheaply if they organise themselves. A group of 15–20 people, usually women of one neighbourhood, saves small amounts regularly, lends to its own members at low interest, and after a year or two of regular saving becomes eligible for a bank loan without collateral — because the group, not an individual, is responsible for repayment and members monitor each other. SHGs thus solve the collateral problem, provide timely loans at reasonable rates, and also give women a platform to discuss health, nutrition and domestic violence.

7.
NCERT exercise3 marks

What are the reasons why the banks might not be willing to lend to certain borrowers?

Model answer

Because those borrowers cannot provide collateral or proper documents, have no regular income or salary record, and are seen as high-risk. Small farmers, landless workers and casual labourers therefore find bank loans difficult, and turn to informal lenders.

8.
NCERT exercise5 marks

In what ways does the Reserve Bank of India supervise the functioning of banks? Why is this necessary?

Model answer

The RBI monitors that banks maintain a minimum cash balance out of deposits; it sees that banks lend not just to profit-making businesses but also to small cultivators, small-scale industries and small borrowers; and it requires banks to submit information periodically on how much they lend, to whom and at what interest rate. This is necessary because banks hold only about 5 per cent of deposits as cash and lend the rest — without supervision, depositors’ money and fair access to credit would both be at risk.

9.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Analyse the role of credit for development.

Model answer

Credit allows production to happen before income arrives: Salim completes a large order because he can buy leather and pay workers in advance, and farmers buy seeds and fertiliser before harvest. It can therefore raise output, incomes and employment. But credit can also harm: if the borrower faces high risk, high interest or crop failure, debt grows and assets are sold, as with Swapna. Whether credit helps development depends on the terms of credit, the risk in the situation and whether there is support in case of loss. Cheap, widely available formal credit is therefore crucial for development.

10.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Manav needs a loan to set up a small business. On what basis will Manav decide whether to borrow from the bank or the moneylender? Discuss.

Model answer

He will compare the terms of credit: the interest rate (a bank may charge 10–12 per cent a year, a moneylender 3–5 per cent a month), the collateral and documents required (a bank will want them; a moneylender may not), the repayment schedule and flexibility, and the risk of unfair recovery. If he has collateral and papers, the bank is far cheaper; if not, he may have to use the moneylender — which is exactly why SHGs and formal credit expansion matter.

11.
NCERT exercise5 marks

In India about 80 per cent of farmers are small farmers who need credit for cultivation. (a) Why might banks be unwilling to lend to small farmers? (b) What other sources can they borrow from? (c) Explain with an example how the terms of credit can be unfavourable for the small farmer. (d) Suggest ways by which small farmers can get cheap credit.

Model answer

(a) Because they lack collateral and proper documents, have small and uncertain incomes, and are seen as high-risk. (b) Moneylenders, agricultural traders, landlords or employers, relatives and friends, and cooperatives. (c) Shyamal pays 3 per cent a month and must sell his crop to the trader who lent to him, so he loses the higher price later in the season. (d) Through cooperative societies and SHGs, Kisan Credit Card-type bank lending, crop loans at low interest with storage receipt facilities, and timely institutional credit instead of trader credit.

12.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Fill in the blanks: (i) Majority of the credit needs of the ___ households are met from informal sources. (ii) ___ costs of borrowing increase the debt-burden. (iii) ___ issues currency notes on behalf of the Central Government. (iv) Banks charge a higher interest rate on loans than what they offer on ___. (v) ___ is an asset that the borrower owns and uses as a guarantee until the loan is repaid.

Model answer

(i) poor (ii) High (iii) Reserve Bank of India (iv) deposits (v) Collateral.

13.
NCERT exercise2 marks

Choose the most appropriate answer. (i) In an SHG most of the decisions regarding savings and loan activities are taken by: (a) Bank (b) Members (c) Non-government organisation. (ii) Formal sources of credit do not include: (a) Banks (b) Cooperatives (c) Employers.

Model answer

(i) (b) Members. (ii) (c) Employers — employers are an informal source.

14.
NCERT exercise5 marks

The following table shows people in a variety of occupations in urban areas. What are the purposes for which they might need loans? Fill in the column, then classify them into two groups — those who might get a bank loan and those who might not. What criterion did you use?

Model answer

For example: construction worker — illness, rent, tools; graduate student who is computer literate — course fees, a laptop; government employee — house, car, children’s education; migrant labourer in Delhi — travel home, rent, emergencies; household maid — school fees, illness; small trader — stock, shop rent; autorickshaw driver — buying or repairing the vehicle; worker whose factory has closed — household expenses until a new job. Likely to get a bank loan: the government employee, the graduate student (education loan), the small trader with records, the autorickshaw driver (vehicle loan against the vehicle). Likely not: the construction worker, migrant labourer, household maid and the retrenched factory worker. Criterion: regular documented income and collateral/security.

09

Important Questions and Answers

Board-style practice

Practice questions

Written in the style of CBSE board papers. They are additional practice, not NCERT originals.

1.

Why is money called a medium of exchange? (2 marks)

Model answer

Because it acts as an intermediate in the exchange process: a person holding money can exchange it for any commodity or service, so sellers need not find a buyer who has exactly the goods they want. Money therefore eliminates the double coincidence of wants.

2.

Explain the modern forms of money. (5 marks)

Model answer

Currency: paper notes and coins. Unlike grain, cattle or gold coins, modern currency has no use of its own; it is accepted because it is authorised by the government. In India the Reserve Bank of India issues currency notes on behalf of the central government, no one else may issue currency, and the law makes the rupee a medium of payment that cannot be refused. Demand deposits: money kept in bank accounts that can be withdrawn on demand; banks pay interest on them, and through cheques they can be used to settle payments without cash. Since demand deposits are widely accepted as a means of payment, they — along with currency — constitute money in the modern economy. Both forms are closely linked to the working of the banking system.

3.

How do banks perform the role of intermediaries? (3 marks)

Model answer

They accept deposits from people with surplus money and pay interest; they keep about 5 per cent as cash for withdrawals and lend the major portion to borrowers who need funds, charging a higher interest. The difference between the two rates is their main income. Thus they mediate between depositors and borrowers.

4.

What is credit? Explain with the two examples of Salim and Swapna how credit can be useful or harmful. (5 marks)

Model answer

Credit is an agreement in which the lender supplies the borrower with money, goods or services in return for a promise of future payment. Salim takes credit — leather on credit and an advance from a trader — to meet working capital needs, completes a large order on time, makes a profit and repays: credit plays a positive role. Swapna borrows from a moneylender for cultivation; pests destroy the crop, the debt grows, and she must sell part of her land — a debt trap. Whether credit helps depends on the risk in the situation and whether there is support in case of loss.

5.

What are the terms of credit? Explain each. (5 marks)

Model answer

Interest rate — the charge the borrower pays along with the principal. Collateral — an asset the borrower owns (land, building, vehicle, livestock, bank deposits) offered as a guarantee; if repayment fails the lender may sell it. Documentation requirement — papers such as employment records and salary slips, as Megha had to provide. Mode of repayment — monthly instalments, repayment after harvest, or repayment through labour. Together these comprise the terms of credit, and they vary with the lender and the borrower.

6.

Compare formal and informal sources of credit. (5 marks)

Model answer

Formal sources are banks and cooperative societies; informal sources are moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives and friends. The RBI supervises formal lenders — checking cash reserves and requiring information on lending — while no organisation supervises informal lenders, who can charge any interest and use unfair means to recover. Informal interest rates are much higher, so a larger part of borrowers’ earnings goes to repayment, sometimes producing a debt trap; formal loans require collateral and documents, which the poor lack. Formal credit meets only about half of rural needs, and richer households get most of it — 83 per cent of rich urban households’ loans are formal against 46 per cent for the poor.

7.

Why are the poor dependent on informal sources of credit? (3 marks)

Model answer

Because banks are not present everywhere in rural India, and even where present, bank loans require proper documents and collateral. Absence of collateral is a major reason the poor cannot get bank loans. Moneylenders know them personally, lend without collateral and are available in an emergency — but charge very high interest, keep no records and harass borrowers.

8.

What are self-help groups? How do they help the poor? (5 marks)

Model answer

SHGs are groups of 15–20 people, usually women of one neighbourhood, who meet and save regularly — Rs 25 to Rs 100 or more per member. Members can take small loans from the group at interest lower than the moneylender’s. After a year or two of regular saving the group becomes eligible for a bank loan, sanctioned in the group’s name, for self-employment — releasing mortgaged land, working capital, housing material, or assets such as a sewing machine, handloom or cattle. The group decides the purpose, amount, interest and repayment, and is responsible for repayment, so banks lend without collateral. SHGs also help women become financially self-reliant and give them a platform to discuss health, nutrition and domestic violence.

9.

Describe the credit arrangements in Sonpur. (5 marks)

Model answer

Shyamal, a small farmer with 1.5 acres, earlier borrowed from the moneylender at 5 per cent a month and now from an agricultural trader at 3 per cent a month, promising to sell his crop to the trader. Arun, a medium farmer with seven acres, is one of the few to get a bank loan at 8.5 per cent a year, repayable within three years, and can later borrow against a cold storage receipt. Rama, a landless labourer, borrows from her employer at 5 per cent a month and repays by working for him, often taking a fresh loan before repaying the old one, and owes Rs 5,000. Nearby, the Krishak Cooperative with 2,300 members accepts deposits, borrows from a bank using them as collateral and lends to members. So credit is available, but its terms differ sharply by who you are.

10.

Why is cheap and affordable credit important for development? (3 marks)

Model answer

Because credit is needed for cultivation, small business and emergencies, and its cost decides whether the borrower gains or loses. Cheap formal credit raises incomes, encourages enterprise and prevents debt traps; expensive informal credit reduces incomes and can force the sale of assets. Hence expanding formal credit and distributing it more equally are both essential for development.

10

Previous Year Questions (PYQs)

Asked in CBSE board exams

Previous year questions

These follow the pattern of questions set in CBSE Social Science papers for this chapter. Answers are model answers.

1.
CBSE pattern

Why are demand deposits considered as money? (CBSE pattern, 2 marks)

Model answer

Because they can be withdrawn on demand and, through cheques, used to settle payments without cash. Since they are widely accepted as a means of payment, they constitute money along with currency.

2.
CBSE pattern

What is collateral? Why do lenders demand it? (2 marks)

Model answer

Collateral is an asset the borrower owns — land, building, vehicle, livestock or bank deposits — used as a guarantee until the loan is repaid. Lenders demand it so that if repayment fails they can sell the asset and recover the money.

3.
CBSE pattern

What is a debt trap? Explain with an example. (3 marks)

Model answer

A situation in which credit pushes a borrower into debt from which recovery is very painful. Swapna borrowed for cultivation, the crop failed because of pests, the debt grew over the year, a fresh loan did not cover the old one, and she had to sell part of her land to repay.

4.
CBSE pattern

Why do banks keep only a small proportion of their deposits as cash? (2 marks)

Model answer

Because on any given day only some depositors come to withdraw money. Banks keep about 5 per cent as cash for these withdrawals and lend the rest, earning the difference between the interest charged on loans and paid on deposits.

5.
CBSE pattern

Explain any two advantages of self-help groups. (2 marks)

Model answer

They provide loans without collateral, since the group guarantees repayment, so the poor can borrow at reasonable interest; and they help women become financially self-reliant while giving them a platform to discuss social issues such as health and domestic violence.

6.
CBSE pattern

State any two differences between formal and informal sources of credit. (2 marks)

Model answer

Formal sources (banks, cooperatives) are supervised by the RBI and charge lower interest; informal sources (moneylenders, traders, employers) are unsupervised and charge much higher interest. Formal loans require collateral and documents; informal loans often do not.

7.
CBSE pattern

Who issues currency notes in India and why is the rupee accepted? (2 marks)

Model answer

The Reserve Bank of India issues currency notes on behalf of the central government, and no other individual or organisation may do so. The law legalises the rupee as a medium of payment that cannot be refused in settling transactions, so it is widely accepted.

8.
CBSE pattern

“Credit may be useful or harmful.” Explain. (3 marks)

Model answer

Credit is useful when it finances production that succeeds, as with Salim, who completes an order and repays with profit. It is harmful when risk is high and support is absent, as with Swapna, whose crop failed and whose debt forced her to sell land. The outcome depends on the risk in the situation and the terms of credit.

9.
CBSE pattern

How does the RBI supervise the functioning of banks? (3 marks)

Model answer

It monitors that banks maintain a minimum cash balance out of deposits, sees that banks lend also to small cultivators, small-scale industries and small borrowers, and requires periodic information on how much is lent, to whom and at what rate.

10.
CBSE pattern

Mention two reasons why the poor depend on informal sources of credit. (2 marks)

Model answer

Banks are not present everywhere in rural India, and bank loans require collateral and proper documents which the poor do not have. Informal lenders know them personally and lend without collateral.

Frequently Asked Questions

Quick clarifications

1.

Why is modern currency accepted when it has no use of its own?

Model answer

Because it is authorised by the government: the RBI issues it, no one else may, and the law makes the rupee a payment that cannot be refused.

2.

What is the difference between currency and demand deposits?

Model answer

Currency is notes and coins held by the public; demand deposits are money kept in bank accounts, withdrawable on demand and usable for payments by cheque.

3.

Who supervises informal lenders?

Model answer

Nobody. There is no organisation supervising their credit activities, which is why they can charge very high interest and use unfair means to recover.

4.

Why can’t the poor get bank loans easily?

Model answer

Because they lack collateral and proper documents, and their incomes are small and irregular. This is why SHGs are important — the group guarantees repayment.

5.

Is a credit card money?

Model answer

It is a means of payment, not money itself: it lets you borrow from the card issuer and repay later. The chapter notes that not all plastic cards are money per se.

6.

What happened in demonetisation?

Model answer

In November 2016 currency notes of Rs 500 and Rs 1,000 were declared invalid and people had to surrender them to banks and receive new notes. Digital transactions through bank transfers, cheques, cards, POS machines and UPI were promoted to reduce the need for cash and control corruption. (Discussed in the chapter’s teacher notes.)

7.

How much cash do Indian banks keep?

Model answer

About 5 per cent of their deposits.

8.

What is the difference between the interest a bank pays and charges?

Model answer

The bank pays interest on deposits and charges a higher rate on loans; the difference is its main source of income.

Assertion-Reason Questions

Choose the correct option

How to answer

(a) Both A and R are true and R explains A. (b) Both are true but R does not explain A. (c) A is true, R is false. (d) A is false, R is true.

1.

Assertion (A): Money removes the need for a double coincidence of wants.
Reason (R): Money acts as an intermediate in the exchange process.

2.

Assertion (A): Modern currency has no use of its own.
Reason (R): It is accepted because it is authorised by the government.

3.

Assertion (A): Demand deposits are a form of money.
Reason (R): They can be withdrawn on demand and used for payments by cheque.

4.

Assertion (A): Banks keep all their deposits as cash.
Reason (R): Banks in India hold about 5 per cent of deposits as cash.

5.

Assertion (A): Credit always benefits the borrower.
Reason (R): In high-risk situations credit can push a borrower into a debt trap.

6.

Assertion (A): Collateral reduces the lender’s risk.
Reason (R): If the borrower fails to repay, the lender can sell the collateral.

7.

Assertion (A): Informal lenders charge higher interest than formal lenders.
Reason (R): There is no organisation supervising the credit activities of informal lenders.

8.

Assertion (A): The Reserve Bank of India supervises cooperative societies and banks.
Reason (R): The RBI issues currency notes on behalf of the central government.

9.

Assertion (A): Self-help groups help the poor overcome the problem of lack of collateral.
Reason (R): Loans are sanctioned in the name of the group, which is responsible for repayment.

10.

Assertion (A): Cheap credit is available to all in India.
Reason (R): The poor depend mainly on informal sources at high interest.

Source-Based and Case-Based Questions

Read the passage or table, then answer

Source 1 — Salim and Swapna

Case study

It is festival season two months from now and the shoe manufacturer, Salim, has received an order from a large trader in town for 3,000 pairs of shoes to be delivered in a month time. To complete production on time, Salim has to hire a few more workers for stitching and pasting work. He has to purchase the raw materials. To meet these expenses, Salim obtains loans from two sources. First, he asks the leather supplier to supply leather now and promises to pay him later. Second, he obtains loan in cash from the large trader as advance payment for 1000 pairs of shoes with a promise to deliver the whole order by the end of the month. At the end of the month, Salim is able to deliver the order, make a good profit, and repay the money that he had borrowed.

Swapna, a small farmer, grows groundnut on her three acres of land. She takes a loan from the moneylender to meet the expenses of cultivation, hoping that her harvest would help repay the loan. Midway through the season the crop is hit by pests and the crop fails. Though Swapna sprays her crops with expensive pesticides, it makes little difference. She is unable to repay the moneylender and the debt grows over the year into a large amount. Next year, Swapna takes a fresh loan for cultivation. It is a normal crop this year. But the earnings are not enough to cover the old loan. She is caught in debt. She has to sell a part of the land to pay off the debt.

1.

In each case, state whether credit was used for production or consumption, and whether it succeeded.

Model answer

Salim used credit for production — working capital for a large order — and succeeded: he delivered, profited and repaid. Swapna used it for production too (cultivation), but the crop failed, so the credit turned into a debt trap and she lost part of her land.

2.

What single difference explains the two outcomes?

Model answer

Risk and support. Salim had a confirmed order and an advance; Swapna faced pests, weather and high interest with no insurance or support if the crop failed.

3.

What would have made Swapna’s situation less risky?

Model answer

Crop insurance, cheaper formal credit, pest-resistant seed and advice, irrigation, and a lender willing to reschedule the loan after a bad season.

Source 2 — The Sonpur field notes

Source extract

Shyamal tells us that every season he needs loans for cultivation on his 1.5 acres of land. Till a few years back, he would borrow money from the village moneylender at an interest rate of five per cent per month (60% per annum). For the last few years, Shyamal has been borrowing from an agricultural trader in the village at an interest rate of three per cent per month. At the beginning of the cropping season, the trader supplies the farm inputs on credit, which is to be repaid when the crops are ready for harvest. Besides the interest charge on the loan, the trader also makes the farmers promise to sell the crop to him.

Arun has seven acres of land. He is one of the few persons in Sonpur to receive bank loan for cultivation. The interest rate on the loan is 8.5 per cent per annum, and can be repaid anytime in the next three years. Rama works as an agricultural labourer. She has to depend on her employer, a medium landowner in Sonpur, for credit. The landowner charges an interest rate of 5 per cent per month. Rama repays the money by working for the landowner.

1.

Compare the annual cost of borrowing for Shyamal, Arun and Rama.

Model answer

Shyamal: 3% a month = about 36% a year (earlier 60%). Arun: 8.5% a year. Rama: 5% a month = about 60% a year, repaid through labour.

2.

Why does the trader insist that farmers sell their crop to him?

Model answer

To ensure prompt repayment — and to profit, because he buys at the low post-harvest price and sells later when prices rise.

3.

What does the difference between Arun and the others show about the credit market?

Model answer

That access to cheap formal credit depends on having land and documents, i.e. collateral. Those without it pay three to seven times as much for credit, which is why formal credit must expand and be shared more equally.

Source 3 — Graph 1: sources of credit in rural India, 2019

How to read this table: each row is one lender type. Add the formal rows and the informal rows separately to see how the market divides.

1.

What share of rural credit comes from formal and from informal sources?

Model answer

Formal: 51 + 10 + 5 = 66 per cent. Informal: 23 + 7 + 3 + 1 = 34 per cent.

2.

Which single informal source is largest, and why does that matter?

Model answer

Moneylenders, at 23 per cent. Since informal interest rates are far higher and unsupervised, a third of rural credit is still very expensive — which reduces borrowers’ incomes and can cause debt traps.

3.

What conclusion does the chapter draw from this graph?

Model answer

That formal credit still meets only about half of rural needs (the chapter says about half, and the graph shows about two-thirds in 2019), so banks and cooperatives must lend more so that dependence on informal credit falls.

1.

This chapter sets no map work. Instead, draw a bar diagram of the 2019 rural credit sources and mark the formal and informal blocks in different colours.

Model answer

Formal block: commercial banks 51, cooperatives 10, other formal 5 = 66%. Informal block: moneylenders 23, relatives 7, other informal 3, landlords 1 = 34%.

2.

Draw a two-bar chart comparing poor and rich urban households’ use of formal and informal credit, and write one conclusion.

Model answer

Poor: 46% formal, 54% informal. Rich: 83% formal, 17% informal. Conclusion: the cheaper the source, the more it is used by the rich — formal credit is unequally distributed.

3.

Prepare a simple flow diagram showing how a self-help group moves from members’ savings to a bank loan.

Model answer

Members save regularly (Rs 25–100+) → group lends small amounts to members at low interest → after 1–2 years of regular saving the group becomes eligible → bank sanctions a loan in the group’s name without collateral → group lends for self-employment → group ensures repayment.

HOTS and Competency-Based Questions

Think beyond the text

Higher order thinking

These ask you to apply, compare or evaluate. Model answers are indicative — your own well-reasoned answer can differ.

1.

Why does a moneylender in a village often know more about a borrower than a bank does, and how does that help and hurt the borrower?

Model answer

He lives in the same village, knows the family, its land, its harvest and its emergencies, and can lend quickly without paperwork or collateral. That helps in a crisis. But it also hurts: because he takes no records and faces no supervision, he can charge 5 per cent a month, insist on buying the crop cheaply, and use unfair means to recover. Personal knowledge substitutes for formal information, but without rules it becomes power over the borrower. (Model answer.)

2.

Should interest rates charged by moneylenders be capped by law? Argue both sides.

Model answer

For: rates of 60 per cent a year are exploitative, keep borrowers poor and can cause debt traps; a cap protects the vulnerable, as RBI supervision does in the formal sector. Against: moneylenders lend without collateral to high-risk borrowers; if a cap makes lending unprofitable they may stop lending altogether, leaving the poor with no credit at all, and enforcement is very difficult because loans are oral and unrecorded. A reasoned answer should weigh protection against the risk of drying up supply, and note that expanding formal credit and SHGs is the surer remedy. (Model answer.)

3.

A student says: “If banks simply gave loans without collateral, poverty would end.” Evaluate.

Model answer

It would help, because lack of collateral is a major reason the poor cannot get cheap credit. But lending without any security raises banks’ risk and could endanger depositors’ money, so the solution has been institutional — SHGs, group liability, cooperative lending — rather than abandoning collateral altogether. And credit alone cannot end poverty: it must be combined with irrigation, markets, education, health and insurance, or a single crop failure produces a Swapna-style debt trap. (Model answer.)

4.

Using Salim and Swapna, explain why the same instrument — credit — produces opposite results.

Model answer

Credit is a claim on future income. Salim’s future income was fairly certain — a confirmed order, an advance, a market for shoes — so borrowing raised his profit. Swapna’s future income depended on a rain-fed crop that pests destroyed, so the loan became a fixed claim on income that did not exist; interest accumulated and she had to sell land. The difference lies in the risk of the activity and whether there is support (insurance, irrigation, rescheduling) when things go wrong. (Model answer.)

5.

Why might a poor household rationally choose a moneylender at 60 per cent over a bank at 10 per cent?

Model answer

Because the bank loan may be unavailable in practice — no collateral, no salary slip, weeks of paperwork, a branch far away — while the moneylender lends in a day, without documents, and will lend again even before the old loan is repaid. In an emergency, availability and speed can matter more than the rate. This is exactly why the chapter argues for expanding formal credit and SHGs rather than blaming the borrower. (Model answer.)

6.

Design a small credit scheme for women in a village with no bank branch. What features would you copy from SHGs and Grameen Bank?

Model answer

Organise 15–20 women per group; require regular small savings; lend first from the group’s own funds; make the group, not the individual, responsible for repayment; sanction bank or federation loans in the group’s name without collateral; keep decisions on purpose, amount and repayment with members; hold weekly meetings that also cover health and nutrition; and add training and a simple record book. These are precisely the features that made Grameen Bank’s borrowers reliable. (Model answer.)

Quick Revision Sheet

One page before the exam

Money

  • Barter needs double coincidence of wants; money is the medium of exchange.
  • Currency: notes and coins, no use of its own, authorised by government; RBI issues it; rupee cannot be refused.
  • Demand deposits: withdrawable on demand, usable by cheque; banks pay interest.

Banks

  • Keep about 5% of deposits as cash; lend the rest.
  • Mediate between depositors and borrowers; income = loan interest − deposit interest.
  • RBI supervises: cash balance, lending to small borrowers, periodic returns.

Credit

  • Credit = money/goods/services now, promise to pay later.
  • Salim: working capital → profit and repayment. Swapna: crop failure → debt trap, land sold.
  • Terms of credit: interest rate, collateral, documentation, mode of repayment.

Sonpur

  • Shyamal: trader at 3%/month, must sell to him (earlier moneylender 5%/month).
  • Arun: bank at 8.5%/year, three years, cold storage receipt loan.
  • Rama: employer at 5%/month, repays with labour, owes Rs 5,000.
  • Krishak Cooperative: 2,300 members, deposits used as collateral for a bank loan.

Formal vs informal

  • Formal: banks, cooperatives; RBI-supervised; cheaper; need collateral.
  • Informal: moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives; unsupervised; expensive.
  • Rural 2019: banks 51%, moneylenders 23%, cooperatives 10%, relatives 7%.
  • Urban: poor 54% informal; rich 17% informal (83% formal).

SHGs and Grameen

  • 15–20 members, savings Rs 25–100+, small loans from the group.
  • After 1–2 years, bank loan in the group’s name without collateral.
  • Decisions by members; group responsible for repayment.
  • Grameen Bank: Yunus, 2006 Nobel Peace Prize; over 9 million members, 81,600 villages (2018).

For development

  • Formal credit must expand and reach the poor equally — cheap credit is crucial for development.
19

Chapter Summary

The whole chapter in a few paragraphs

Money is anything widely accepted as a medium of exchange. In barter, exchange requires a double coincidence of wants; money, by providing an intermediate step, removes that need. Modern money takes two forms: currency — notes and coins which have no use of their own but are accepted because the government authorises them, with the Reserve Bank of India issuing notes on the government’s behalf — and demand deposits with banks, which can be withdrawn on demand and used for payments by cheque.

Banks keep about 5 per cent of deposits as cash and lend the rest, mediating between depositors and borrowers and earning the difference between the two interest rates. The RBI supervises them, checking cash balances and the direction of lending.

Credit — an agreement to supply money, goods or services in return for a promise of future payment — can transform production, as with Salim, who used it as working capital and made a profit, or destroy a household, as with Swapna, whose crop failed and who lost part of her land: a debt trap. The outcome depends on the risk in the situation, the terms of credit (interest rate, collateral, documentation, mode of repayment) and whether there is support in case of loss.

In Sonpur, a small farmer pays 3 per cent a month to a trader and must sell to him, a medium farmer pays 8.5 per cent a year to a bank, and a landless labourer pays 5 per cent a month to her employer. Formal sources — banks and cooperatives — are supervised and cheap but need collateral, so the poor depend on informal sources at far higher cost. Self-help groups, in which 15–20 members save and lend to each other and later obtain bank loans without collateral, show a way forward, as does the Grameen Bank. Expanding formal credit and sharing it more equally are both essential for development.
